QF.id: AIFM CIII AIFs in India and Suitability_7

question.text: Mr. Vivek Saxena, a family-office CIO, is choosing between a Cat III AIF and a PMS. Per Table 4.2, which statement is CORRECT regarding pooling of funds and custody?

answer.text: In PMS, pooling is compulsory and securities are held in a single pooled demat account
Both PMS and Cat III AIF issue units that represent undivided interest in a pooled portfolio
In Cat III AIF, separate demat accounts are opened for each investor reflecting individual ownership
PMS holds securities at individual client level via separate demat accounts; Cat III AIF pools funds compulsorily and trades at fund level

explanation.text: The Logic: Table 4.2: PMS pools only for onboarding/trade execution but securities are held at individual client level in SEPARATE demat accounts — the investor owns the securities directly. Cat III AIF pools COMPULSORILY for collective investment and trades only at the pooled fund level; investors hold UNITS, not underlying securities. The Trap: Options A and C invert the PMS and AIF structures. Option B is wrong — PMS does NOT issue units; it is a direct-ownership model. Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B (Portfolio Manager) exam tests the PMS direct-ownership + separate demat extensively. XIX-E tests the contrast with Cat III's pooled unit structure — critical because this drives the tax treatment difference (PMS = investor-level; Cat III = fund-level MMR). Manager's Pro-Tip: The pooled structure is why Cat III uses HWM crystallisation at the UNIT series level (equalisation) — a PMS manager doesn't need this because each client has their own book. When a new subscriber joins a Cat III fund mid-quarter, issue a NEW series to avoid embedded-gain free-riding.
